section: Where this chapter sits in the course
text:
Where this chapter sits in the course
Chapter 1 described light as a wave, Chapter 2 guided it in fibers and Chapter 3 built a source, the LED, from a forward-biased pn junction. An LED emits by spontaneous emission: every photon has a random phase and direction, and the spectrum is a few \(k_BT\) wide. Chapter 4 adds the third process between light and matter, stimulated emission. It is the basis of optical amplifiers (the erbium-doped fiber amplifier that made long-haul WDM possible, the semiconductor optical amplifier) and of lasers: a gain medium inside an optical resonator. The same three ingredients, a population inversion, an optical gain \(g\) and a cavity with losses \(\alpha_t\), explain the ruby, He–Ne and Nd:YAG lasers as well as the laser diodes that drive every fiber link (Ch. 2) and are detected by the photodiodes of Ch. 5.

title: 1  Radiation in a box
text:
1.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 4–7: radiation in a box at temperature \(T\), counting the modes, the density of modes, the “ultraviolet catastrophe” and Planck’s law.
A cubic box of side \(L\) with conducting walls holds standing waves whose wavevector components are quantised (slide 4),
\[
k_x=\frac{\pi n_x}{L},\quad k_y=\frac{\pi n_y}{L},\quad k_z=\frac{\pi n_z}{L},\qquad n_x,n_y,n_z=1,2,3,\dots
\]
Each triplet \((n_x,n_y,n_z)\) is a point of a cubic lattice in “mode space” (slide 5). A mode of frequency \(\nu\) sits at the distance \(p=\sqrt{n_x^2+n_y^2+n_z^2}=2L\nu/c\) from the origin. Counting the points in the positive octant of a spherical shell of radius \(p\) and thickness \(dp\), and multiplying by 2 for the two polarisations, gives the number of modes per unit volume per unit frequency (slides 6–7):
\[
\frac{dN}{L^3\,d\nu}=\frac{1}{L^3}\cdot2\cdot\frac{1}{8}\cdot4\pi p^2\frac{dp}{d\nu}=\frac{8\pi\nu^2}{c^3}.
\]
Classical physics gives every mode the mean energy \(k_BT\). The energy density per unit frequency is then the Rayleigh–Jeans law, \(\rho(\nu)=8\pi k_BT\nu^2/c^3\), which grows without bound at high frequency: the “disaster at high frequency” of slide 7. Planck replaced \(k_BT\) by the mean energy of a quantised oscillator, \(h\nu/(e^{h\nu/k_BT}-1)\), which falls off exponentially when \(h\nu\gg k_BT\):
\[
\rho_\text{eq}(\nu)=\frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}\,\frac{1}{\exp(h\nu/k_BT)-1}.
\]
The Planck law reappears in Chapter 2: Einstein used it to find the ratio of spontaneous to stimulated emission.

TipGoing further






Density of modes in a medium. In a medium of index \(n\), \(k=2\pi n\nu/c\) and the mode density becomes \(8\pi n^3\nu^2/c^3\) (or \(8\pi n^2n_g\nu^2/c^3\) with dispersion). This \(n^3\) enters \(A_{21}/B_{21}\) and the threshold of semiconductor lasers (Chapter 6).
Spontaneous emission is not a constant of the atom. Fermi’s golden rule makes \(A_{21}\) proportional to the density of modes at \(\nu_{21}\). In a cavity of volume \(V\) and quality factor \(Q\) the rate is multiplied by the Purcell factor \(F_P=\frac{3}{4\pi^2}\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^3\frac{Q}{V}\). title: 2  Absorption, spontaneous and stimulated emission
text:
2.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 8–10 (spontaneous versus stimulated emission, the three decay channels of an excited electron) and 15–19 (Einstein coefficients, laser requirements, spontaneous decay time).
Three processes connect two levels \(E_1<E_2\) through photons of energy \(h\nu=E_2-E_1\) (slides 8–9, 15). Absorption and stimulated emission need a photon; spontaneous emission does not. The stimulated photon is a copy of the incoming one: same direction, same phase, same polarisation (slide 8). With \(\rho(\nu)\) the radiation energy density per unit frequency, the rates per unit volume are
\[
R_{12}=B_{12}N_1\rho(\nu),\qquad R_{21}=A_{21}N_2+B_{21}N_2\rho(\nu).
\]
In thermal equilibrium \(R_{12}=R_{21}\), the populations follow Boltzmann, \(N_2/N_1=e^{-h\nu/k_BT}\), and \(\rho\) must be Planck’s law (Chapter 1). This is only possible for every \(T\) if (slides 16–17)
\[
B_{12}=B_{21},\qquad \frac{A_{21}}{B_{21}}=\frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}\quad\left(\times n^3\text{ in a medium of index }n\right).
\]
Two ratios follow and they are the two laser requirements of slide 18:
\[
\frac{R_{21}(\text{stim})}{R_{12}(\text{abs})}=\frac{N_2}{N_1}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{population inversion},\qquad
\frac{R_{21}(\text{stim})}{R_{21}(\text{spon})}=\frac{c^3}{8\pi h\nu^3}\rho(\nu)\ \Rightarrow\ \text{optical cavity}.
\]
Without other processes, the upper level empties at the rate \(A_{21}\): \(N_2(t)=N_2(0)e^{-t/\tau_{sp}}\) with \(\tau_{sp}=1/A_{21}\) (slide 19). In a real medium the excited electron also decays non-radiatively (slide 10), so the measured lifetime is \(1/\tau=1/\tau_{sp}+1/\tau_{nr}\) and only the fraction \(\tau/\tau_{sp}\) of the decays emits light.

2.3 From lifetime to Einstein coefficients
The spontaneous lifetime is the measured quantity. The \(B\) coefficient follows from \(A_{21}/B_{21}\). The ratio grows as \(\nu^3\): at short wavelengths spontaneous emission becomes fast and steals the inversion. This is one reason why the first stimulated-emission device was a microwave maser (1954), and why X-ray lasers are so hard.

section: 2.4 Stimulated versus spontaneous emission: the cavity
text:
2.4 Stimulated versus spontaneous emission: the cavity
In thermal equilibrium the ratio stimulated/spontaneous is \(1/(e^{h\nu/k_BT}-1)\), about \(10^{-33}\) for red light at 300 K (Chapter 1). A cavity traps the emitted photons and raises \(\rho(\nu)\) in a few modes by many orders of magnitude. The figure shows the photon density needed for stimulated emission to win:


Show the Python
nu, dnu = lz.c0/632.8e-9, 1.5e9
Nph = np.logspace(10, 20, 200)
rho = Nph*lz.h*nu/dnu
ratio = rho/lz.A_over_B(nu)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.6))
ax.loglog(Nph, ratio)
ax.axhline(1, color=lz.INK2, ls="--", lw=1.2); ax.axvline(2.1e15, color=lz.PALETTE[1], lw=1.2)
ax.text(2.4e15, 1e-4, "He–Ne laser\n(slide 73)", fontsize=8, color=lz.PALETTE[1])
ax.set(xlabel="photon density N_ph (m⁻³)", ylabel="R(stim)/R(spon) per atom"); plt.show()
print(f"stimulated = spontaneous at N_ph = {lz.A_over_B(nu)*dnu/(lz.h*nu):.2e} m^-3")








Figure 2.1: Ratio of stimulated to spontaneous emission rates, c³ρ(ν)/(8πhν³), versus photon density in the mode volume for a transition at 632.8 nm with a 1.5 GHz linewidth (ρ ≈ N_ph hν/Δν, slide 64). Inside a He–Ne laser N_ph ≈ 2×10¹⁵ m⁻³ (slide 73).





stimulated = spontaneous at N_ph = 3.14e+14 m^-3


Inside the He–Ne laser the ratio is about 7: thanks to the mirrors, stimulated emission wins. The ratio \(c^3\rho/8\pi h\nu^3\) is the number of photons per mode: \(N_\text{ph}\) divided by the number of modes per unit volume within the linewidth, \(8\pi\nu^2\Delta\nu/c^3=3\times10^{14}\) m⁻³. The cavity does not fill every mode. It selects one (or a few) modes and lets the photons pile up there. The spontaneous emission into all the other modes is lost: it limits the efficiency and adds noise (Chapter 19).






TipGoing further






Degenerate levels. If \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) have degeneracies \(g_1\), \(g_2\), detailed balance gives \(g_1B_{12}=g_2B_{21}\) and the inversion condition becomes \(N_2/g_2>N_1/g_1\). Redo the derivation of slide 16 with degeneracies.
From \(A_{21}\) to a cross section. For a transition with a normalised lineshape \(g(\nu)\), the emission cross section is \(\sigma_{em}(\nu)=\dfrac{\lambda^2}{8\pi n^2\tau_{sp}}g(\nu)\) (Füchtbauer–Ladenburg). Check the order of magnitude of the Er³⁺ value used in Chapter 4: \(\lambda=1.53\) µm, \(\tau_{sp}=10\) ms, \(\Delta\nu\approx4\) THz.
Which \(B\)? Some books define \(B\) with the intensity \(I\), the photon flux or the angular frequency instead of \(\rho(\nu)\). The numerical values differ by \(c/n\), \(h\nu\) or \(2\pi\). Always check the definition before using a tabulated value.
Non-radiative channels (slide 10). Multiphonon emission depends on how many phonons bridge the gap \(E_2-E_1\). This “energy-gap law” explains why the Er³⁺ \(^4I_{13/2}\) level (0.8 eV) is long-lived in silica but the \(^4I_{11/2}\) pump level decays in microseconds.

A. Einstein, “Zur Quantentheorie der Strahlung”, Physikalische Zeitschrift 18, 121 (1917): the original argument.
Kasap, sec. 4.1–4.2; Svelto, Principles of Lasers, 5th ed., ch. 2.
R. Loudon, The Quantum Theory of Light, ch. 1–2: why stimulated photons are identical.

title: 3  Three- and four-level lasers
text:
3.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 11–14 (the laser principle with the ruby laser, three-level lasers, the four-level Nd:YAG laser) and 20–21 (worked example: minimum pump power of a three-level laser).
A two-level system cannot be inverted (Chapter 2). Real lasers use auxiliary levels (slides 11–14):
With a pump rate \(W_p\) per ground-state ion and fast decay from the pump level, the steady-state inversions are
\[
\text{3-level: }\ \frac{N_2-N_1}{N_0}=\frac{W_p\tau_{sp}-1}{W_p\tau_{sp}+1},\qquad
\text{4-level: }\ \frac{N_2-N_1}{N_0}=\frac{W_p(\tau_{21}-\tau_{10})}{1+W_p(\tau_{21}+\tau_{10})}\approx W_p\tau_{21}.
\]
The three-level system needs \(W_p\tau_{sp}>1\): every ion must be pumped faster than it decays, which gives the minimum pump power of slide 20,
\[
\frac{P_{p,\min}}{V}=\frac{N_0}{2}\,\frac{h\nu_{13}}{\tau_{sp}}.
\]

title: 3  Three- and four-level lasers
text:
Three-level laser (ruby, Cr³⁺:Al₂O₃). Pump photons lift ions from the ground state \(E_1\) to a broad band \(E_3\). The ions relax in picoseconds, through phonons, to the long-lived level \(E_2\) (\(\tau_{sp}=3\) ms). The laser transition \(E_2\to E_1\) ends on the ground state, so more than half of all ions must be pumped before any gain appears.
Four-level laser (Nd³⁺:YAG). The laser transition ends on a level \(E_1\) that lies about 0.25 eV above the ground state and empties in nanoseconds. \(E_1\) is almost empty at room temperature, so every ion that reaches \(E_2\) (\(\tau_{sp}=230\) µs) already contributes to the inversion.

section: 3.4 A flash-pumped ruby laser in time
text:
3.4 A flash-pumped ruby laser in time
The panel above shows steady states. A flash lasts about 1 ms, comparable to \(\tau_{sp}\). The figure integrates the three-level rate equation \(dN_2/dt=W_p(t)N_1-N_2/\tau_{sp}\) for a Gaussian flash:


Show the Python
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
tau = 3e-3
t = np.linspace(0, 6e-3, 2000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8))
for Wmax in (300, 800, 2000):
    W = lambda t: Wmax*np.exp(-4*np.log(2)*((t - 1.5e-3)/1e-3)**2)
    s = solve_ivp(lambda t, y: [W(t)*(1 - y[0]) - y[0]/tau], (0, t[-1]), [0.0], t_eval=t, max_step=1e-5)
    ax.plot(t*1e3, s.y[0], label=f"peak W_p = {Wmax} s⁻¹ (W_pτ = {Wmax*tau:.1f})")
ax.axhline(0.5, color=lz.PALETTE[7], ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax2 = ax.twinx(); ax2.fill_between(t*1e3, np.exp(-4*np.log(2)*((t - 1.5e-3)/1e-3)**2), color=lz.GRID, alpha=0.5, zorder=0)
ax2.set_yticks([]); ax2.grid(False); ax.set_zorder(ax2.get_zorder() + 1); ax.patch.set_visible(False)
ax.set(xlabel="time (ms)", ylabel="N₂/N₀", ylim=(0, 1)); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right"); plt.show()

title: 4  Optical gain and the erbium-doped fiber amplifier
text:
4.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 22–24 (absorption and emission cross sections, optical gain coefficient), 25–42 (the EDFA: energy levels, cross sections, configurations, gain versus pump power, fiber length and output power, power conversion efficiency, pump length, worked example, gain equalisation) and 43–44 (noise figure, ASE).
An ion in the lower level absorbs a fraction of the light that crosses it, as if it presented an opaque area, the absorption cross section \(\sigma_{ab}\) (slide 22). An ion in the upper level adds stimulated photons with an emission cross section \(\sigma_{em}\) (slide 23). In a slab of thickness \(\delta x\), with \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) ions per unit volume, the intensity changes by \(\delta I/I=(\sigma_{em}N_2-\sigma_{ab}N_1)\delta x\). This defines the optical gain coefficient (slide 24),
\[
g(\nu)=\sigma_{em}(\nu)N_2-\sigma_{ab}(\nu)N_1,\qquad G=\frac{P_\text{out}}{P_\text{in}}=\exp(gL).
\]
In the EDFA (slides 25–28), Er³⁺ ions in silica glass absorb a 980 nm pump into the \(^4I_{11/2}\) level, which decays in microseconds to the metastable \(^4I_{13/2}\) level (\(\tau_{sp}\approx10\) ms). Signals in the C band (1530–1565 nm) are amplified by stimulated emission back to the ground state \(^4I_{15/2}\). Each level is split into a manifold of Stark sublevels, so \(\sigma_{ab}(\lambda)\) and \(\sigma_{em}(\lambda)\) are broad and different: absorption dominates at short wavelengths, emission at long ones (slide 28a). With the fractional inversion \(x=N_2/N_0\) (slide 39),
\[
g=\left[\sigma_{em}x-\sigma_{ab}(1-x)\right]N_0 .
\]
Energy conservation bounds the output (slides 36–37). The power conversion efficiency \(\eta_\text{PCE}=(P_{s,\text{out}}-P_{s,\text{in}})/P_{p,\text{in}}\) cannot exceed \(\lambda_p/\lambda_s\) (one signal photon per pump photon at best), so
\[
G=1+\eta_\text{PCE}\frac{P_{p,\text{in}}}{P_{s,\text{in}}},\qquad
P_{s,\text{in}}<\frac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_s}\,\frac{P_{p,\text{in}}}{G-1}.
\]
The pump is absorbed as it travels. It can keep all the ions in a length \(L_p\) inverted only if it delivers \(N_0h\nu_p\) per unit volume every \(\tau_{sp}\) (slide 38): \(\Gamma P_p\approx AN_0h\nu_pL_p/\tau_{sp}\), with \(\Gamma\) the fraction of pump power that overlaps the doped core.

text:
4.3 The EDFA along the fiber
The uniform-inversion model ignores that the pump weakens along the fiber. The panel solves the steady-state two-level rate equations at every point. The local inversion is set by the local pump and signal photon fluxes,
\[
x(z)=\frac{\sigma_{ab,p}\Phi_p+\sigma_{ab,s}\Phi_s}{(\sigma_{ab,p}+\sigma_{em,p})\Phi_p+(\sigma_{ab,s}+\sigma_{em,s})\Phi_s+1/\tau_{sp}},
\qquad \Phi_k=\frac{\Gamma_kP_k}{h\nu_kA},
\]
and each power grows or decays as \(dP_k/dz=\Gamma_k[\sigma_{em,k}x-\sigma_{ab,k}(1-x)]N_0P_k\) (forward pumping, no ASE).

section: 4.5 Going further: noise figure and amplified spontaneous emission (slides 43–44)
text:
4.5 Going further: noise figure and amplified spontaneous emission (slides 43–44)
Slide 43 defines the noise figure \(\text{NF}=\text{SNR}_\text{in}/\text{SNR}_\text{out}\) but does not say where the noise comes from. Ions in the upper level also emit spontaneously into the guided mode. These photons are amplified like the signal, and form the broad amplified spontaneous emission (ASE) pedestal of slide 44a. In a bandwidth \(B_o\) and two polarisations, the ASE power at the output is
\[
P_\text{ASE}=2n_{sp}(G-1)h\nu B_o,\qquad n_{sp}=\frac{\sigma_{em}N_2}{\sigma_{em}N_2-\sigma_{ab}N_1}\ge1 .
\]
The spontaneous-emission factor \(n_{sp}\) equals 1 only at full inversion. When the amplified signal beats with the ASE on a photodiode (Ch. 5), the dominant noise is the signal–spontaneous beat noise, and
\[
\text{NF}\approx2n_{sp}\frac{G-1}{G}+\frac1G\ \xrightarrow{G\gg1}\ 2n_{sp}\ \ge\ 2\ (3\text{ dB}).
\]
No phase-insensitive amplifier can do better than 3 dB: amplifying a coherent state necessarily adds noise (Caves, 1982).

  GdB: Inputs.range([5, 40], {value: 25, step: 0.5, label: "gain G (dB)"}),
  Bo: Inputs.range([0.01, 1], {value: 0.1, step: 0.01, label: "optical bandwidth B_o (nm)"})
})

  return {nsp, NF, Pase, ok: e*nf.x > a*(1 - nf.x)};
}

The noise figure is lowest where the inversion is highest, which is at the pump input end of the fiber. This is why low-noise pre-amplifiers are forward pumped at 980 nm (full inversion possible) while booster amplifiers can be backward pumped or use 1480 nm pumps (higher PCE, but \(x<1\) because the pump also stimulates emission). Slide 44b shows the other effect: when the input power rises, the signal saturates the inversion, \(n_{sp}\) grows and the NF increases.

5.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 45–53 (the He–Ne laser: principle, modes, other lasing lines, efficiency example), 54–60 (Doppler broadening and the mode-counting example) and 61–62 (the argon-ion laser).
In the He–Ne laser (slides 45–47) an electrical discharge excites helium atoms into the metastable \(2^1S_0\) and \(2^3S_1\) states. Their energies (20.61 and 19.82 eV) almost coincide with the Ne \(3s_2\) and \(2s_2\) levels, so a collision hands the energy over, \(\text{He}^*+\text{Ne}\to\text{He}+\text{Ne}^*\). The excited Ne atoms are inverted with respect to the short-lived \(2p\) levels. The \(3s_2\to2p_4\) transition gives the red line at 632.8 nm; other transitions give the green, yellow, orange and infrared lines of slide 52.
The two mirrors at distance \(L\) form a Fabry–Perot resonator. Only standing waves with a whole number of half wavelengths fit (slides 48–49):
\[
m\frac{\lambda_m}{2n}=L,\qquad \nu_m=m\frac{c}{2nL},\qquad \Delta\nu_m=\frac{c}{2nL},\qquad \Delta\lambda_m\approx\frac{\lambda^2}{2nL}.
\]
The output spectrum is the product of these longitudinal modes with the optical gain curve of the medium. In a gas the gain curve is Doppler broadened: atoms moving toward the mirror see a blue-shifted frequency, atoms moving away a red-shifted one. The Maxwell velocity distribution makes the curve Gaussian with FWHM (slide 49)
\[
\Delta\nu_{1/2}=2\nu_0\sqrt{\frac{2k_BT\ln2}{Mc^2}},\qquad \Delta\lambda_{1/2}\approx\Delta\nu_{1/2}\frac{\lambda}{\nu}.
\]

The He–Ne laser converts less than 0.1 % of its electrical power into light. The Ar⁺ laser is worse: the laser levels sit 35 eV above the neutral ground state (slide 62), while each photon carries only 2.5 eV, and kilowatts of heat must be carried away by water cooling. Both lasers have been replaced by laser diodes and diode-pumped solid-state lasers in most applications. The He–Ne survives where its spectral purity and wavelength accuracy matter (interferometry, metrology).






TipGoing further






Mode competition in an inhomogeneous medium. Each longitudinal mode interacts with its own velocity class of atoms, at \(\pm v=c(\nu_m-\nu_0)/\nu_0\). Modes do not steal each other’s atoms, so several modes lase together. Compare with the homogeneously broadened Nd:YAG laser in Chapter 7.
Lamb dip. A mode tuned exactly to \(\nu_0\) interacts with the \(v=0\) atoms in both directions of travel, so it has fewer atoms available than a slightly detuned mode. The output power versus cavity tuning shows a dip at line centre, used to stabilise He–Ne lasers to about \(10^{-9}\).
Brewster windows. The tube windows are tilted at Brewster’s angle (Ch. 1): the p polarisation passes without loss, the s polarisation loses about 15 % per pass. Compute the round-trip loss of each polarisation with the Fresnel equations and show why the output is linearly polarised.
Isotope shift. ²⁰Ne and ²²Ne lines differ by about 900 MHz at 632.8 nm. Commercial tubes use a mixture to broaden the gain curve. Model the gain as the sum of two Gaussians.

text:
6.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 63–68 (gain coefficient and population inversion, threshold gain, phase condition, output versus pump rate), 69 and 74 (threshold inversion of the He–Ne laser), 70–73 (output power and photon cavity lifetime). Also the two exercises of the course MATLAB live script Chapter4.mlx.
The gain coefficient is the fractional power increase per unit length (slide 64). Writing the net stimulated emission rate \((N_2-N_1)B_{21}\rho\) with \(\rho\approx N_\text{ph}h\nu_0/\Delta\nu\) gives the peak gain in terms of the inversion,
\[
g(\nu_0)\approx(N_2-N_1)\frac{B_{21}nh\nu_0}{c\,\Delta\nu}.
\]
A wave that makes one round trip in a cavity of length \(L\), with mirror reflectances \(R_1\), \(R_2\) and internal loss \(\alpha_s\), returns with the power \(P_f=P_iR_1R_2e^{2gL}e^{-2\alpha_sL}\). Steady oscillation needs \(P_f=P_i\) (slide 65): the gain must equal the total loss,
\[
g_{th}=\alpha_t=\alpha_s+\frac{1}{2L}\ln\frac{1}{R_1R_2}.
\]
The phase must also repeat after a round trip, \(nk_m\,2L=2\pi m\) (slide 67), which selects the longitudinal modes of Chapter 5. With \(A_{21}/B_{21}\) from Chapter 2, the threshold inversion is (slide 66)
\[
(N_2-N_1)_{th}\approx g_{th}\frac{8\pi n^2\nu_0^2\tau_{sp}\Delta\nu}{c^2}.
\]
Photons leave the cavity through the mirrors and are absorbed inside it. The photon population decays with the photon cavity lifetime (slide 72) and the output power is the photon flux through mirror 1 (slide 71):
\[
\tau_{ph}=\frac{2nL}{c\left[1-e^{-2\alpha_tL}\right]}\approx\frac{n}{c\,\alpha_t},\qquad
P_o=\tfrac12A(1-R_1)h\nu_0N_\text{ph}\frac{c}{n}.
\]
Above threshold the inversion is clamped at \((N_2-N_1)_{th}\). Every extra pump excitation becomes a stimulated photon, so \(P_o\) grows linearly with the pump rate (slide 68).

for beta, c in zip((1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-6), lz.PALETTE):
    # steady state (units N_th = τ_sp = τ_ph = 1 for N and rates; S in units of N_th τ_ph/τ_sp):
    # N(1 + S) = Rp  and  S(N − 1) + βN = 0  →  S = βN/(1 − N); solve the quadratic for N
    a, b, cc = (1 - beta), -(1 + Rp), Rp           # (1 − β)N² − (1 + Rp)N + Rp = 0
    N = (-b - np.sqrt(b**2 - 4*a*cc))/(2*a)
    S = beta*N/(1 - N)
    ax[0].plot(Rp, N, color=c, label=f"β = {beta:g}")
    ax[1].loglog(Rp, S, color=c, label=f"β = {beta:g}")
ax[0].plot(Rp, np.minimum(Rp, 1), ":", color=lz.INK2, lw=1.2, label="ideal")
ax[0].set(xlabel="pump rate R_p/R_th", ylabel="inversion N/N_th"); ax[0].legend(fontsize=8)
ax[1].set(xlabel="pump rate R_p/R_th", ylabel="photons in the mode S"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()








Figure 6.1: Steady state of the rate equations versus pump rate (normalised to threshold, R_th = N_th/τ_sp). Left: inversion N/N_th, which clamps at 1 above threshold (slide 68). Right: photon number S (log scale) for three values of β. A smaller β gives a sharper threshold: the jump in S across threshold is about 1/β.





Gas and solid-state lasers have \(\beta\sim10^{-8}\) to \(10^{-10}\) and a razor-sharp threshold. Laser diodes have \(\beta\sim10^{-4}\) to \(10^{-5}\). Microcavity and nanolasers approach \(\beta\to1\), the “thresholdless” laser, where the kink disappears and only photon statistics distinguish laser light from spontaneous emission.

7.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slide 75 (transverse laser modes) and slides 76–83 (homogeneous and inhomogeneous broadening, Lorentzian and Gaussian line shapes, Doppler broadening, spectral hole burning, summary table).
Transverse modes (slide 75). Real mirrors are curved and finite, so the field that reproduces itself after a round trip is not a plane wave but a Gaussian beam (Ch. 1) multiplied by Hermite polynomials. The TEM\(_{mn}\) mode has \(m\) nodes along \(x\) and \(n\) along \(y\):
\[
E_{mn}(x,y)\propto H_m\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2x}{w}\right)H_n\!\left(\frac{\sqrt2y}{w}\right)\exp\!\left(-\frac{x^2+y^2}{w^2}\right).
\]
TEM\(_{00}\) is the Gaussian beam with the smallest divergence; most lasers are designed to emit only this mode.
Line broadening (slides 76–83). An emitting transition is never infinitely sharp.
When both act, the line is their convolution, the Voigt profile.

title: 7  Transverse modes and line broadening
text:
Homogeneous broadening affects all atoms in the same way: lifetime (natural) broadening, collisions in a gas, phonon collisions in a crystal. A field that decays as \(E_0e^{-t/2\tau_2}\cos\omega_0t\) has a Lorentzian spectrum (slides 77–78), \[g_L(\nu)=\frac{\gamma/\pi}{(\nu-\nu_0)^2+\gamma^2},\qquad \Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\gamma=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau_2}.\]
Inhomogeneous broadening gives different atoms different centre frequencies: Doppler shifts in a gas, random local fields in a glass. The line is the envelope of many narrow lines, usually a Gaussian (slides 79–80), \[g_G(\nu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\nu-\nu_0)^2}{\Gamma^2}\right],\qquad \Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\Gamma\sqrt{\ln2}.\]








WarningLifetime broadening on slide 78





Slide 78 writes “\(1/\gamma=\tau_2\)” with \(\Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=2\gamma\). For the field \(E_0e^{-t/2\tau_2}\cos\omega_0t\) written on the same slide, the Fourier transform gives a Lorentzian with \(\Delta\nu_\text{FWHM}=1/(2\pi\tau_2)\), that is \(\gamma=1/(4\pi\tau_2)\). The statement \(1/\gamma=\tau_2\) holds for the angular half width when the field (not the intensity) decays with \(\tau_2\). The factor \(4\pi\) matters: a 100 ns Ne level has a natural width of 1.6 MHz, not 20 MHz. Slide 80 also writes the normalisation as \(\int g_L\,d\nu=1\) under the Gaussian; it should read \(g_G\).

  const N = 2001, span = 12, dx = 2*span/(N - 1), xs = d3.range(N).map(i => -span + i*dx);

title: 8  Q-switching and mode-locking
text:
8.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 84–87 (Q-switching: principle, time sequence, commercial Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers, rotating prism, saturable absorber and electro-optic switches) and 88 (mode-locking).
Q-switching (slides 84–87). The quality factor \(Q\) of the cavity is kept low (a mirror is blocked or misaligned) while the pump builds up an inversion \(N_i\) far above the normal threshold \(N_{th}\). The medium stores energy because its upper level is long-lived (ms for Nd:YAG and ruby, Chapter 2). Then \(Q\) is switched high in nanoseconds. The photon density grows from spontaneous noise at the rate \((N/N_{th}-1)/\tau_c\), where \(\tau_c\) is the photon lifetime of the high-\(Q\) cavity, and a giant pulse empties the inversion. Without pumping during the pulse, the four-level rate equations in normalised form (\(n=N/N_{th}\), time in units of \(\tau_c\)) are
\[
\frac{dn}{dt}=-n\phi,\qquad \frac{d\phi}{dt}=(n-1)\phi .
\]
Their solution gives the fraction \(\eta\) of the stored inversion that is extracted, from \(r\eta=-\ln(1-\eta)\) with \(r=N_i/N_{th}\), and the peak photon density \(\phi_\text{max}=r-1-\ln r\) (in units of \(N_{th}\)), reached when \(n=1\).
Mode-locking (slide 88). A laser oscillating on \(N\) longitudinal modes spaced by \(\delta\nu=c/2L\) emits their sum. If the phases are random, the output is noisy around its average. If the phases are locked (equal), the modes add in phase once per round trip \(T=2L/c\) and produce a train of pulses of width
\[
\Delta t\approx\frac{T}{N}\approx\frac{1}{\Delta\nu},\qquad P_\text{peak}\approx N\,P_\text{average}.
\]
The pulse width is set by the gain bandwidth \(\Delta\nu\): the broader the gain, the shorter the pulse.

8.2 The giant pulse


Show the Python

viewof qs = Inputs.form({
  r: Inputs.range([1.05, 10], {value: 3, step: 0.05, label: "initial inversion r = N_i/N_th"}),
  tc: Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 10, step: 1, label: "photon lifetime τ_c (ns)"}),
  phi0: Inputs.range([-12, -3], {value: -8, step: 0.5, label: "log₁₀ initial photon density (spontaneous seed)"})
})


















Show the Python
qsOut = {
  const tEnd = 30*Math.max(1, 4/(qs.r - 1)) + 20;
  const sol = rk4((t, [n, p]) => [-n*p, (n - 1)*p], [qs.r, 10 ** qs.phi0], 0, tEnd, 6000, 10);
  const data = sol.flatMap(({t, y}) => [{t: t*qs.tc, v: y[0], who: "inversion n = N/N_th"}, {t: t*qs.tc, v: y[1], who: "photon density φ (units of N_th)"}]);
  const ph = sol.map(d => d.y[1]), pk = d3.max(ph), ipk = ph.indexOf(pk);
  const above = sol.filter(d => d.y[1] >= pk/2), fw = (above[above.length - 1].t - above[0].t)*qs.tc;
  // solve r η = −ln(1 − η) by bisection
  let a = 1e-9, b = 1 - 1e-12; for (let i = 0; i < 100; i++) { const c = (a + b)/2; if (qs.r*c + Math.log(1 - c) > 0) a = c; else b = c; }
  return {data, pk, tpk: sol[ipk].t*qs.tc, fw, eta: (a + b)/2, nf: sol[sol.length - 1].y[0]};
}
Plot.plot({
  width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 300, x: {label: "time after the Q-switch (ns)"}, y: {label: "normalised value", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#eb6834", "#2a78d6"]},
  marks: [Plot.line(qsOut.data, {x: "t", y: "v", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2}), Plot.ruleY([1], {stroke: "#52514e", strokeDasharray: "3,3"})]
})

The inversion falls below threshold at the end (\(n_f<1\)): the photons present at the peak keep stimulating emission while they leak out.
A larger \(r\) gives a shorter, stronger and earlier pulse. Near \(r=1\) the pulse is long and weak: Q-switching only pays off when the stored inversion is many times threshold.

8.3 Mode-locking (slide 88)


Show the Python
viewof ml = Inputs.form({
  N: Inputs.range([1, 101], {value: 15, step: 1, label: "number of oscillating modes N"}),
  L: Inputs.range([0.1, 2], {value: 1.5, step: 0.05, label: "cavity length L (m)"}),
  locked: Inputs.radio(["locked (equal phases)", "random phases"], {value: "locked (equal phases)", label: "phases"}),
  seed: Inputs.range([1, 50], {value: 7, step: 1, label: "random seed"}),
  shape: Inputs.radio(["equal amplitudes", "Gaussian gain envelope"], {value: "equal amplitudes", label: "mode amplitudes"})
})









Show the Python
mlOut = {
  const c = 299792458, T = 2*ml.L/c, dnu = 1/T;
  let s = ml.seed*9301 + 49297; const rnd = () => (s = (s*9301 + 49297) % 233280)/233280;
  const ph = d3.range(ml.N).map(() => ml.locked.startsWith("locked") ? 0 : 2*Math.PI*rnd());
  const amp = d3.range(ml.N).map(k => ml.shape.startsWith("equal") ? 1 : Math.exp(-((k - (ml.N - 1)/2)**2)/(2*(ml.N/4 + 0.5)**2)));
  const P = amp.reduce((a, b) => a + b*b, 0), data = [];
  for (let i = 0; i <= 1500; i++) {
    const t = 3*T*i/1500; let re = 0, im = 0;
    for (let k = 0; k < ml.N; k++) { const a = 2*Math.PI*(k - (ml.N - 1)/2)*dnu*t + ph[k]; re += amp[k]*Math.cos(a); im += amp[k]*Math.sin(a); }
    data.push({t: t*1e9, I: (re*re + im*im)/P});
  }
  const peak = d3.max(data, d => d.I);
  return {data, T, dnu, peak};
}

How are the phases locked? Active mode-locking modulates the loss (or the gain) at exactly \(c/2L\) (the EO switch of slide 88c): each mode acquires sidebands that coincide with its neighbours and injection-locks them. Passive mode-locking uses a saturable absorber, or the Kerr lens of the gain crystal (Ti:sapphire), which favours high peak intensity. Write the field as a sum of modes with a sinusoidal loss modulation and iterate it round trip by round trip.

Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 89–91 (degenerately doped pn junction, population inversion under forward bias, gain versus photon energy) and 128–130 (optical gain curve, gain spectra of InGaAsP versus carrier density, peak gain versus carrier density).
In a semiconductor the “two levels” are two bands. Under forward bias, electrons injected into the conduction band and holes in the valence band each reach their own equilibrium, described by the quasi-Fermi levels \(E_{Fn}\) and \(E_{Fp}\) of Chapter 3, with \(E_{Fn}-E_{Fp}=eV\) (slide 90). A photon of energy \(h\nu\) connects a conduction state \(E_2\) with a valence state \(E_1\) with \(E_2-E_1=h\nu\). Stimulated emission beats absorption when the upper state is more likely full than the lower state, \(f_c(E_2)>f_v(E_1)\), which reduces to the Bernard–Duraffourg condition
\[
E_g<h\nu<E_{Fn}-E_{Fp}=eV .
\]
The quasi-Fermi levels must penetrate into the bands: in a homojunction this requires degenerate doping on both sides (slide 90); in a double heterostructure the injected carriers themselves do it (Chapter 10). The gain spectrum (slide 91) is the absorption spectrum of the unpumped crystal multiplied by the inversion factor,
\[
g(h\nu)=\alpha_0(h\nu)\left[f_c(E_2)-f_v(E_1)\right],
\]
with \(\alpha_0\propto\sqrt{h\nu-E_g}\) for parabolic bands. Gain is positive between \(E_g\) and \(\Delta F=E_{Fn}-E_{Fp}\), zero at \(h\nu=\Delta F\) (transparency of that photon energy) and negative (absorption) above. As the carrier density \(n\) grows, \(\Delta F\) moves up, the gain band widens and its peak shifts to higher energies (slide 129).

Dashed: free-carrier model for GaAs with no broadening and with 30 meV Gaussian broadening. The model reproduces the sharp onset near transparency, but at a density about 0.3–0.5×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ lower than the measured GaAs curve, and it rises far more steeply.

The free-carrier model shows the physics but overestimates the gain: it neglects the light-hole band, intraband scattering (which broadens each transition by about 10 meV), many-body effects such as bandgap renormalisation, and the polarisation dependence of the matrix element. For design numbers, the slides use measured or fully modelled curves (slide 130), and so does the example of Chapter 12. Near threshold, a linear or logarithmic fit is common:
\[
g_\text{peak}\approx a\,(n-n_{tr})\quad\text{or}\quad g_\text{peak}\approx g_0\ln\frac{n}{n_{tr}},
\]
with the differential gain \(a=dg/dn\approx1\)–\(3\times10^{-16}\) cm² for bulk GaAs and transparency density \(n_{tr}\approx1\)–\(1.5\times10^{18}\) cm⁻³. The differential gain sets the modulation speed (Chapter 16).






TipGoing further






Add the light holes. The valence band has heavy (\(m^*\approx0.5m_e\)) and light (\(m^*\approx0.08m_e\)) holes. Compute \(E_{Fp}\) with both bands and add the two gain contributions. How much does the transparency density change?
Gain and spontaneous emission are linked. The same Fermi factors give the spontaneous spectrum \(r_{sp}\propto\alpha_0f_c(1-f_v)\), and \(g(h\nu)=r_{sp}(h\nu)\,[1-e^{(h\nu-\Delta F)/k_BT}]\times\text{const}\) (McCumber/van Roosbroeck–Shockley). Measuring the spontaneous spectrum gives the gain (Hakki–Paoli method uses the FP fringes instead).
Refractive index change. Gain and refractive index are linked by Kramers–Kronig. The change \(dn/dN\) of the index with carrier density causes the linewidth enhancement factor \(\alpha_H\) and the chirp of directly modulated lasers (Chapter 19).

10.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 92–100 (homojunction laser, output characteristic, double heterostructure, stripe geometry, buried heterostructures, commercial devices), 101–102 (example: modes and cavity length) and 103–107 (beam characteristics, output spectra, temperature dependence of threshold and wavelength, example on \(d\lambda/dT\)).
The first laser diodes (Hall et al., 1962, slide 93) were GaAs homojunctions: a degenerately doped pn junction with two cleaved facets as mirrors (slide 92). The facets reflect \(R=[(n-1)/(n+1)]^2\approx0.32\), enough because the gain is huge. But the injected carriers spread over a diffusion length (µm) and the light is not guided, so the threshold current density was about 500 A mm⁻² at room temperature (slide 94 notes): only pulsed operation, or cryogenic cooling.
The double heterostructure (DH, slides 95–96) sandwiches a thin (0.1–0.2 µm) narrow-gap active layer between wide-gap claddings. The band offsets confine the carriers, and the higher index of the active layer guides the light (the planar waveguide of Ch. 2; carrier and photon confinement were introduced for LEDs in Ch. 3 and enter the threshold through Γ in Chapter 12). Thresholds dropped to a few A mm⁻², and in 1970 Hayashi and Panish, and Alferov’s group, obtained continuous operation at room temperature. Stripe contacts (slide 97) restrict the current to a few µm width; buried heterostructures (slides 98–99) surround the active region by low-index, wide-gap material on all sides, which also guides the light laterally and keeps one transverse mode.
The cavity selects longitudinal modes (slides 101–102, as in Chapter 5):
\[
m\frac{\lambda_m}{2n}=L,\qquad \Delta\lambda_m\approx\frac{\lambda^2}{2n_gL},
\]
where strictly the group index \(n_g=n-\lambda\,dn/d\lambda\approx4.3\) should replace \(n\) (the slides use \(n=3.6\)).
The threshold rises exponentially with temperature (slide 105), and the wavelength drifts (slides 106–107):
\[
I_{th}=A\exp\!\left(\frac{T}{T_0}\right),\qquad
\frac{d\lambda_m}{dT}\approx\frac{\lambda_m}{n}\frac{dn}{dT}\ \text{(one mode)},\qquad
\frac{d\lambda_\text{peak}}{dT}\approx-\frac{\lambda^2}{hc}\frac{dE_g}{dT}\ \text{(gain peak)}.
\]

The near field of an edge emitter is an ellipse about 1 µm × 3 µm. Diffraction (Ch. 1) makes the far field an ellipse rotated by 90°: the beam diverges fastest in the direction where it is narrowest. Above threshold every extra electron becomes a stimulated photon with probability \(\eta_\text{IDQE}\) (close to 1), and that photon leaves through the output facet with probability \(\eta_\text{EE}\). Hence (slide 114)
\[
P_o=\eta_\text{EE}\,\eta_\text{IDQE}\,\frac{h\nu}{e}(I-I_{th}),\qquad
\eta_\text{slope}=\eta_\text{EE}\,\eta_\text{IDQE}\,\frac{h\nu}{e},\qquad
\eta_\text{EDQE}=\eta_\text{EE}\,\eta_\text{IDQE}.
\]
The EQE is always smaller than the EDQE, because the threshold current pumps the medium without producing coherent light.

title: 12  The laser diode equation
text:
12.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 123–127 (the rate equations of a double-heterostructure laser, threshold, output power, threshold gain with the confinement factor Γ) and 131–134 (worked example: threshold current and output power of a GaAs DH Fabry–Perot laser).
A current \(I\) injects electrons into an active layer of length \(L\), width \(W\) and thickness \(d\) (slide 123). Two rate equations balance them (slide 124):
\[
\frac{I}{eLWd}=\frac{n}{\tau_r}+Cn\,N_\text{ph},\qquad\frac{N_\text{ph}}{\tau_{ph}}=Cn\,N_\text{ph}.
\]
Electrons are supplied by the current and removed by spontaneous (\(n/\tau_r\)) and stimulated (\(CnN_\text{ph}\)) recombination. Coherent photons are created by stimulated emission and lost from the cavity with the photon lifetime \(\tau_{ph}\) of Chapter 6. As long as \(N_\text{ph}\neq0\), the second equation fixes the carrier density at
\[
n_{th}=\frac{1}{C\tau_{ph}},\qquad \frac{I_{th}}{eLWd}=\frac{n_{th}}{\tau_r}\qquad\text{(slide 125)}.
\]
Above threshold \(n\) stays clamped at \(n_{th}\), and all the extra current becomes photons (slides 125–126):
\[
N_\text{ph}=\frac{\tau_{ph}}{eLWd}(I-I_{th}),\qquad
P_o=\left[\frac{hc^2\tau_{ph}(1-R)}{2en\lambda L}\right](I-I_{th}).
\]
The threshold density \(n_{th}\) is the density at which the gain reaches threshold. Only the fraction \(\Gamma\) of the mode that overlaps the active layer sees the gain (slide 127), so
\[
\Gamma g_{th}=\alpha_t=\alpha_s+\frac{1}{2L}\ln\frac{1}{R_1R_2},
\]
and \(n_{th}\) follows from the gain curve \(g(n)\) of slide 130 (Chapter 9).

title: 13  Quantum-well lasers
text:
13.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 135–136 (single and multiple quantum-well lasers, step-like density of states, light confinement) and 137–139 (worked example: levels and emission wavelength of a GaAs quantum well).
When the active layer is thinner than about 20 nm, the motion of the carriers across it is quantised (Chapter 3, quantum wells). For an infinite well of width \(d\) the electron and hole levels above the band edges are
\[
\varepsilon_n=\frac{h^2n^2}{8m_e^*d^2},\qquad \varepsilon'_{n'}=\frac{h^2n'^2}{8m_h^*d^2},
\]
and the radiative transitions obey the selection rule \(\Delta n=n-n'=0\). The emitted photon is therefore
\[
h\nu=E_g+\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon'_1 .
\]
The density of states becomes a staircase that is finite at the band edge (slide 135c). Carriers fill the first sub-band instead of spreading over a \(\sqrt E\) band, so inversion is reached with fewer carriers, the gain spectrum is narrower and the threshold current is lower. The well is too thin to guide light: a single quantum well (SQW) overlaps only a few percent of the mode. Multiple quantum wells (MQW, slide 136) or a separate-confinement heterostructure (SCH, a wider waveguide around the well) restore the optical confinement.

Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 140–144 (distributed Bragg reflector and distributed feedback lasers, commercial devices, example on the DFB wavelength), 145–146 (external cavity laser diodes) and 147–151 (vertical cavity surface emitting lasers).
A Fabry–Perot laser diode oscillates on several modes, and hops between them (Chapter 10). WDM systems (Ch. 2) need one wavelength, stable to a fraction of 0.8 nm. The solution is a mirror whose reflectance depends on wavelength: a Bragg grating (Ch. 1, Bragg mirrors; Ch. 2, fiber Bragg gratings). A corrugation of period \(\Lambda\) reflects strongly only near the Bragg wavelength (slide 140b)
\[
\lambda_B=\frac{2n\Lambda}{q},\qquad q=1,2,\dots\ \text{(order)}.
\]

title: 14  Single-frequency lasers: DBR, DFB, external cavity, VCSEL
text:
In a DBR laser (slide 140) the gratings replace the facets, outside the pumped region.
In a DFB laser (slides 141–142) the grating runs along the whole active region: feedback is distributed. A uniform grating does not lase at \(\lambda_B\) but on two modes just outside the stop band (slide 142), \[\lambda_m=\lambda_B\pm\frac{\lambda_B^2}{2nL}(m+1).\] An asymmetry (a facet coating, or a quarter-wave phase shift in the middle of the grating) selects one of them.
An external cavity laser (slides 145–146) uses an AR-coated diode chip, a lens and an external grating or filter: long cavity, narrow linewidth (kHz), tunable.
A VCSEL (slides 147–151) has a cavity about one wavelength long between two epitaxial DBR mirrors. The mode spacing is so large that only one longitudinal mode fits under the gain curve, but the single-pass gain is tiny, so the mirrors need \(R>99\) %.

title: 15  Semiconductor optical amplifiers and superluminescent LEDs
text:
15.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 152–158 (semiconductor optical amplifiers: travelling-wave and Fabry–Perot types, gain saturation, polarisation-dependent gain, commercial devices) and 159–161 (superluminescent LEDs).
A laser diode below threshold is an amplifier: light that enters one facet leaves the other amplified by the single-pass gain \(G_s=e^{(\Gamma g-\alpha_s)L}\). Two versions exist (slides 155–157):
The gain saturates when the signal depletes the carriers (slide 155c). For a homogeneously broadened medium, \(G=G_0\exp[-(G-1)P_\text{in}/P_\text{sat}]\), and the output at which the gain has dropped by 3 dB, \(P_{o,\text{sat}}\), is quoted in datasheets (slide 158). Because the carrier lifetime is ~0.1–1 ns, the SOA gain follows the bit pattern, unlike the EDFA (Chapter 4): this causes cross-talk between WDM channels, but also enables all-optical wavelength conversion.
A superluminescent LED (SLED, slides 159–161) is an SOA with no input: spontaneous emission generated at one end is amplified on its way out, with feedback suppressed by angled facets, an absorbing section or AR coatings. The output is bright and directional like a laser but broadband and incoherent like an LED.

title: 15  Semiconductor optical amplifiers and superluminescent LEDs
text:
The travelling-wave (TW) SOA has anti-reflection coated (and often angled) facets: one pass, broad and smooth gain spectrum (30–60 nm), about 20–30 dB.
The Fabry–Perot (FP) SOA keeps reflecting facets: a regenerative amplifier, whose gain is enhanced at the cavity resonances and suppressed between them, \[G_{FP}=\frac{(1-R_1)(1-R_2)G_s}{\left(1-\sqrt{R_1R_2}\,G_s\right)^2+4\sqrt{R_1R_2}\,G_s\sin^2\phi},\] with \(\phi\) the single-pass phase. The gain ripple is \(\left[(1+\sqrt{R_1R_2}G_s)/(1-\sqrt{R_1R_2}G_s)\right]^2\).

title: 16  Modulation of laser diodes
text:
16.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 162–163 (direct modulation, small-signal response and relaxation-oscillation frequency) and 164 (digital modulation: turn-on delay, relaxation oscillations, biasing near threshold).
The output of a laser diode follows its current, so the simplest transmitter modulates the current directly (slide 162): a DC bias \(I_1\) above threshold plus a modulation \(\Delta I_m\sin(2\pi ft)\). The rate equations of Chapter 12 couple two reservoirs, carriers (\(\tau\)) and photons (\(\tau_{ph}\)). Like a mass on a spring they exchange energy and oscillate at the relaxation-oscillation frequency (slide 163)
\[
f_r\approx\frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{\tau\tau_{ph}}}\left(\frac{I_1}{I_{th}}-1\right)^{1/2}.
\]
Linearising the rate equations gives the small-signal response, a damped second-order system,
\[
H(f)=\frac{\Delta P(f)}{\Delta P(0)}=\frac{\omega_r^2}{\omega_r^2-\omega^2+j\omega\gamma},\qquad \omega_r=2\pi f_r,\qquad
\gamma=\frac{I_1/I_{th}}{\tau}.
\]
It is flat at low frequency, peaks near \(f_r\) and falls at 40 dB/decade above. Raising the bias raises \(f_r\) and the bandwidth (slide 163). For large-signal (digital) modulation from \(I_1<I_{th}\) to \(I_2>I_{th}\), the carriers must first build up to \(n_{th}\) before any stimulated emission appears (slide 164). With \(dn/dt=I_2/eV-n/\tau\) this takes the turn-on delay
\[
t_d=\tau\ln\frac{I_2-I_1}{I_2-I_{th}} .
\]
Biasing just below or at threshold (\(I_1\to I_{th}\)) removes the delay.

title: 16  Modulation of laser diodes

WarningThe turn-on delay formula in the slide-164 notes





The speaker notes give \(t_d=\tau\ln[I_2/(I_2-(I_{th}-I_1))]\). Integrating \(dn/dt=I_2/eV-n/\tau\) from \(n_1=I_1\tau/eV\) to \(n_{th}=I_{th}\tau/eV\) gives \(t_d=\tau\ln[(I_2-I_1)/(I_2-I_{th})]\). The two agree only for \(I_1=0\). For \(I_1=0.8I_{th}\), \(I_2=2I_{th}\) the notes give \(0.11\tau\) and the correct value is \(0.18\tau\).

title: 17  Holography
text:
17.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 165–168: Gabor’s invention, wavefront recording (the hologram) and wavefront reconstruction (virtual and real images).
A photograph records the intensity \(|E|^2\) of the light scattered by an object and loses its phase, which carries the depth. Holography (Gabor, 1948, slide 165) records the phase too, by letting the object wave \(U(x,y)\) interfere with a known reference wave \(U_r(x,y)\) (slide 167). The film records
\[
I(x,y)=|U_r+U|^2=|U_r|^2+|U|^2+U_r^*U+U_rU^* .
\]
After development its amplitude transmittance is proportional to \(I\). Illuminating it with the reference wave again (slide 168) transmits
\[
U_rI=\underbrace{U_r\left(|U_r|^2+|U|^2\right)}_\text{zero order}+\underbrace{|U_r|^2\,U}_\text{object wave: virtual image}
+\underbrace{U_r^2\,U^*}_\text{conjugate wave: real image}.
\]
The third term is a copy of the object wave: an observer sees the object, in 3D, behind the hologram. The fourth term is the phase conjugate: it converges to a real image in front of the hologram. Recording needs coherence: the path difference between object and reference must stay below the coherence length (Ch. 1), and the fringes must not move by more than a fraction of their period during the exposure. This is why practical holography waited for the laser (1962, Leith and Upatnieks).
Leith and Upatnieks tilted the reference by an angle \(\theta\) (off-axis holography). The fringes then have period \(\lambda/\sin\theta\), and the three reconstructed waves leave the hologram in different directions, so the images do not overlap.

18.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Not in the slides. Slide 75 shows transverse modes and slide 48 the longitudinal modes of a cavity, but the chapter never asks which mirrors make a cavity work, how large the beam is, or at which frequencies the transverse modes oscillate. This chapter answers these questions with the Gaussian beams of Chapter 1.
A Gaussian beam (Ch. 1) has a waist \(w_0\) and a wavefront radius \(R(z)=z[1+(z_R/z)^2]\), with \(z_R=\pi w_0^2/\lambda\). It is a mode of a two-mirror cavity if, at each mirror, its wavefront curvature matches the mirror curvature. With the stability parameters
\[
g_1=1-\frac{L}{R_1},\qquad g_2=1-\frac{L}{R_2}\qquad(R=\infty\text{ for a flat mirror}),
\]
such a beam exists only if
\[
0\le g_1g_2\le1 \qquad\text{(stable resonator)}.
\]
Its size on the mirrors and at the waist are
\[
w_1^2=\frac{\lambda L}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g_2}{g_1(1-g_1g_2)}},\quad
w_2^2=\frac{\lambda L}{\pi}\sqrt{\frac{g_1}{g_2(1-g_1g_2)}},\quad
w_0^2=\frac{\lambda L}{\pi}\frac{\sqrt{g_1g_2(1-g_1g_2)}}{|g_1+g_2-2g_1g_2|}.
\]
The Hermite–Gauss modes TEM\(_{mn}\) (slide 75) accumulate an extra Gouy phase \((m+n+1)\arccos\sqrt{g_1g_2}\) per pass, so their resonance frequencies are
\[
\nu_{qmn}=\frac{c}{2nL}\left[q+(m+n+1)\frac{\arccos(\pm\sqrt{g_1g_2})}{\pi}\right],
\]
with the sign of \(g_1\) (and \(g_2\)). Transverse modes thus add frequencies between the longitudinal modes of Chapter 5.

  const g1 = 1 - L/R1, g2 = 1 - L/R2, G = g1*g2, stable = G >= 0 && G < 1 && !(g1 === 0 && g2 !== 0) && !(g2 === 0 && g1 !== 0);
  const s = lam*L/Math.PI;

18.3 Why stability matters for lasers
The mode volume \(\approx\pi w_0^2L/2\) decides how many atoms contribute to the gain, and the mode size on the mirrors decides how much light is clipped by the apertures. Near the stability edges (\(g_1g_2\to0\) or \(1\)) the mode becomes very small or very large and sensitive to misalignment. Most lasers are designed well inside the stable region. High-power lasers with large-volume, high-gain media sometimes use unstable resonators on purpose: the beam fills the medium, and the output leaves around the edge of a small mirror.






TipGoing further






ABCD matrices. Write the round-trip matrix \(M\) of the cavity (propagation, mirror, propagation, mirror). Stability is \(|A+D|/2\le1\), and the self-consistent \(q\) parameter solves \(q=(Aq+B)/(Cq+D)\). Check that this reproduces \(w_1\) above, then add a thermal lens (Chapter 3) inside the cavity.
Laser diodes. Edge-emitter waveguides guide the mode, so the stability analysis is replaced by the waveguide modes of Ch. 2. In an external-cavity laser (Chapter 14), the lens and grating form an ABCD system again.
Fox–Li iteration. Propagate an arbitrary field back and forth between two finite mirrors with the angular-spectrum method (the holography code of Chapter 17) and watch it converge to TEM\(_{00}\), with a diffraction loss per pass that depends on the Fresnel number \(a^2/\lambda L\).

title: 19  Going further: laser linewidth, noise and chirp
text:
19.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Not in the slides. The tables of slides 143 and 149 quote linewidths from 50 kHz to 0.1 nm, and the notes of slide 163 mention “chirping”, but the chapter does not explain what limits the linewidth of a single-mode laser, or why directly modulated lasers change colour. This chapter connects the rate equations (Chapter 12, Chapter 16) with coherence (Ch. 1) and fiber dispersion (Ch. 2).
Linewidth. Even a perfectly single-mode laser is not monochromatic. Each spontaneous photon that enters the lasing mode adds a field of random phase to the coherent field. The phase performs a random walk, and the line acquires a Lorentzian shape whose width is the Schawlow–Townes linewidth, modified for a laser above threshold:
\[
\Delta\nu=\frac{\pi h\nu\,(\Delta\nu_c)^2\,n_{sp}}{P_\text{out}}\,(1+\alpha_H^2),\qquad \Delta\nu_c=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau_{ph}}.
\]
The linewidth falls as \(1/P\) and as \(\tau_{ph}^2\): a long, low-loss cavity helps quadratically. In semiconductor lasers the linewidth enhancement factor \(\alpha_H=-\frac{4\pi}{\lambda}\frac{dn/dN}{dg/dN}\approx3\)–6 (Henry, 1982) multiplies the width by \(1+\alpha_H^2\approx10\)–40: every fluctuation of the carrier density changes the refractive index and therefore the phase.
Intensity noise. The same spontaneous events make the power fluctuate. The relative intensity noise (RIN) peaks at the relaxation-oscillation frequency \(f_r\) (Chapter 16) and decreases at high power; its floor is the shot-noise limit \(\text{RIN}_\text{SQL}=2h\nu/P\).
Chirp. When the current changes, the carrier density changes, and with it the index. The optical frequency follows the power transients (Koch and Linke):
\[
\Delta\nu(t)=\frac{\alpha_H}{4\pi}\left[\frac{d\ln P}{dt}+\kappa P\right],
\]
where the first term is transient chirp and the second, from gain compression, adiabatic chirp.

Chirp converts the clean intensity pulse into a pulse whose leading and trailing edges have different wavelengths. Fiber dispersion (Ch. 2) then moves them apart. This is why 1550 nm links above 2.5 Gb/s over more than a few tens of km use a CW DFB laser followed by an external modulator (Mach–Zehnder or electro-absorption, Ch. 6), whose chirp is close to zero.

20.4 Improvements to the course

One equation, three lasers. The threshold condition \(\Gamma g_{th}=\alpha_s+\frac{1}{2L}\ln\frac{1}{R_1R_2}\) and the rate equations explain the He–Ne, the Nd:YAG and the laser diode. The threshold calculator of Chapter 6 puts them side by side: a gain of 0.1 m⁻¹ versus 5000 m⁻¹, photon lifetimes of 30 ns versus 2 ps.
“Predict, then compute.” “If I double the facet reflectance, does the slope efficiency go up or down?”, “Which side of the EDFA gain spectrum disappears first when the inversion drops?”, “Does a Q-switched pulse leave the inversion above or below threshold?”
Fill the missing derivations. Slides 43 (noise figure), 75 (transverse modes) and 88 (mode-locking) state results without the physics; the noise-figure section of Chapter 4 and the two Going further chapters can be used as handouts.
Lab connection. A laser diode on a TEC mount, a power meter and a cheap spectrometer cover threshold, slope efficiency, \(T_0\), mode hops and the mode spacing. A He–Ne laser and a scanning Fabry–Perot show longitudinal and transverse modes.
Modern content. Possible updates: silicon photonics lasers (heterogeneous III–V on Si), quantum-dot and quantum-cascade lasers, frequency combs, high-power fiber lasers, lidar VCSEL arrays, laser safety classes (IEC 60825-1).

20.5 Notes for the instructor: checks on the slides
While recomputing the examples, everything matched the slides (ruby pump power, EDFA example, He–Ne Doppler and threshold examples, laser-diode modes, efficiencies, threshold current and output power, QW and DFB examples) except these points:

Slide numbering: the 2024 PDF (Chapter4 - Lasers_2024.pdf, 159 pages) does not follow the 2025 .pptx (170 slides). The companion uses the .pptx numbers.
Slide 6: \(dN=4\pi\nu(L/c)^3d\nu\) should be \(4\pi\nu^2(L/c)^3d\nu\) (one polarisation). Slides 6–7 then use \(4\pi k_BT\nu^2/c^3\), while Planck’s law on slide 7 has \(8\pi\): the factor 2 for the two polarisations is missing (Chapter 1).
Slide 58: the mode number is printed “1.264,222.5” (i.e. 1,264,222.5).
Slide 78: “\(1/\gamma=\tau_2\)” with \(\Delta\nu=2\gamma\) contradicts the field \(E_0e^{-t/2\tau_2}\cos\omega_0t\) on the same slide, which gives \(\Delta\nu=1/(2\pi\tau_2)\), i.e. \(\gamma=1/(4\pi\tau_2)\) (Chapter 7). Slide 80: the normalisation box shows \(\int g_L\) instead of \(\int g_G\).
Slide 111: the definition under “Internal Quantum Efficiency” is labelled \(\eta_\text{IDQE}\); the differential efficiency is defined on slide 112.
Slide 116: for the 500 mW red laser, \(P_o/(I-I_{th})=500/(700-400)=1.67\) mW/mA, not the 1.0 quoted; all other rows are consistent (Chapter 11).
Slide 133: \(n_{th}\approx2.5\times10^{18}\) cm⁻³ for \(g=111\) cm⁻¹ is read from the figure; the curve of slide 130 gives about \(2.4\times10^{18}\) cm⁻³. The results (30 A mm⁻², 37.5 mA) are consistent with 2.5.
Slide 139: the finite-well values (0.031, 0.121, 0.007 eV, 848 nm) are about 5 % below a direct solution with the stated parameters (0.033, 0.126, 0.006 eV, 850 nm) (Chapter 13).
Slide 143: the footnote “fm is \(10^{-15}\) s” should read \(10^{-15}\) m.
Slide 149: for the 680 nm single-mode VCSEL, \(P_o/(I-I_{th})=0.95/2.6=0.37\) mW/mA versus 0.32 quoted (minor).
Slide 164, speaker notes: \(t_d=\tau\ln[I_2/(I_2-(I_{th}-I_1))]\) is correct only for \(I_1=0\); the general result is \(t_d=\tau\ln[(I_2-I_1)/(I_2-I_{th})]\) (Chapter 16).
Slides 43–44: the noise figure is defined but not derived; the companion adds \(\text{NF}\approx2n_{sp}\) and the ASE power (Section 4.5).
Slide 101: the mode spacing uses the phase index (3.6); measured FP spacings follow the group index (\(\approx4.3\) for GaAs), about 20 % smaller (Chapter 10).
